title: Translational kinetic energy
body: K = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.1 "An object's translational kinetic energy is given by the equation K = 1/2 mv^2"

title: Kinetic energy is a scalar and depends on reference frame
body: Translational kinetic energy is a scalar, and different observers may measure different values of K for the same object depending on their frame of reference.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2, 3.1.A.3 "Different observers may measure different values of the translational kinetic energy"

title: Work
body: Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system by a force exerted on that system over a distance.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 "Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system by a force exerted on that system over a distance"

title: Work done by a variable force (line integral)
body: W = \int_{a}^{b} \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.3 "The work done on an object by a variable force is calculated using ... the integral is taken over the path from point a to point b"

title: Dot product magnitude
body: \vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = AB\cos\theta
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.3.i "The dot product between two vectors, A and B, results in a scalar quantity"

title: Work by a force with constant parallel component
body: W = F_{\parallel} d = F d\cos\theta
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.3.iii "If the component of the force ... parallel to the displacement is constant, the work done ... is given by the derived equation"

title: Only the parallel force component changes the system's energy
body: Only the component of force parallel to the displacement of the point of application changes the system's total energy, while a perpendicular component can change the direction of motion without changing kinetic energy.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.3.ii, 3.2.A.3.iv "can change the direction of the system's motion without changing the system's kinetic energy"

title: Work is a scalar with sign
body: Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.2 "Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero"

title: Work–energy theorem
body: \Delta K = \sum_i W_i = \sum_i F_{\parallel,i}\, d_i
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.4 "The work–energy theorem states that the change in an object's kinetic energy is equal to the sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces"

title: Conservative force work
body: The work done by a conservative force is path-independent, depends only on the initial and final configurations, and is zero if the system returns to its initial configuration.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.i, 3.2.A.1.ii "path-independent and only depends on the initial and final configurations"

title: Nonconservative force work
body: The work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent, and the most common nonconservative forces are friction and air resistance.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.iv, 3.2.A.1.v "The work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent"

title: Potential energy only for conservative forces
body: Potential energies are associated only with conservative forces.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.iii "Potential energies are associated only with conservative forces"

title: Energy dissipated by friction
body: E_{\text{dissipated}} = F_{f}\, \ell_{\text{path}}
caution: Use the length of the path traveled (not just net displacement) since friction work is path-dependent.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.4.iii "equated to the force of friction times the length of the path over which the force is exerted"

title: Work as area under an F∥ vs. displacement graph
body: Work equals the area under the curve of a graph of F∥ as a function of displacement.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.5 "Work is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of F|| as a function of displacement"

title: Boundary: mechanical energy only
body: Only the transfer of mechanical energy is analyzed, though students should be aware that mechanical energy may be dissipated as thermal energy or sound.
ced_evidence: BOUNDARY STATEMENT "only expects students to analyze the transfer of mechanical energy"

title: Potential energy change from a conservative force
body: \Delta U = -\int_{a}^{b} \vec{F}_{cf}\cdot d\vec{r}
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.4 "The relationship between conservative forces exerted on a system and the system's potential energy"

title: Force from potential energy
body: F_{x} = -\frac{dU(x)}{dx}
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.5 "Fx = −dU(x)/dx"; forces point in the direction of decreasing potential energy

title: Potential energy of a system
body: A system of two or more objects has potential energy if the objects interact only through conservative forces, and it is a scalar associated with the positions of objects in the system.

title: Zero of potential energy is a choice
body: The definition of zero potential energy is a decision made by the observer to simplify or assist analysis.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.3 "a decision made by the observer"

title: Stable equilibrium
body: Stable equilibrium is a location at which a small displacement results in a force opposite to the displacement, accelerating the object back toward equilibrium; it occurs at a local minimum of U(x).
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.6.i, 3.3.A.6.iii "local minimum"

title: Unstable equilibrium
body: Unstable equilibrium is a location at which a small displacement results in a force in the same direction as the displacement, accelerating the object away from equilibrium; it occurs at a local maximum of U(x).
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.6.ii, 3.3.A.6.iv "local maximum"

title: Elastic potential energy of an ideal spring
body: U_{s} = \tfrac{1}{2} k (\Delta x)^{2}
caution: U_s is never negative; it does not change sign between stretched and compressed.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.7.i "elastic potential energy of an ideal spring ... Δx is the distance the spring has been stretched or compressed"

title: Gravitational potential energy near a planet's surface
body: \Delta U_{g} = m g \Delta y
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.7.iii "change in gravitational potential energy ... may be approximated by the equation"

title: Potential energy of multi-object systems
body: The total potential energy of a system with more than two objects is the sum of the potential energy of each pair of objects.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.8 "sum of the potential energy of each pair of objects"

title: Which systems can have which energies
body: A system of a single object can only have kinetic energy, while a system with objects interacting via conservative forces or that can change shape reversibly may have both kinetic and potential energies.

title: Mechanical energy
body: E_{\text{mech}} = K + U
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.1 "Mechanical energy is the sum of a system's kinetic and potential energies"

title: Energy balance within and across system boundaries
body: Any change to one type of energy in a system must be balanced by an equivalent change in other types within the system or by a transfer of energy between the system and its surroundings.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.2, 3.4.B.4 "equivalent to the energy transferred into or out of the system"

title: System choice determines whether energy changes
body: If the work done on the selected system is zero and there are no nonconservative interactions within it, total mechanical energy is constant; if the work is nonzero, energy is transferred between the system and the environment.
caution: Energy is conserved in all interactions; state the chosen system when claiming mechanical energy is or is not constant.
ced_evidence: 3.4.C.1, 3.4.C.2, 3.4.C.3 "Energy is conserved in all interactions"

title: Boundary: dissipation by nonconservative forces
body: Students must know that mechanical energy can be dissipated as thermal energy or sound by nonconservative forces.
ced_evidence: BOUNDARY STATEMENT "mechanical energy can be dissipated as thermal energy or sound by nonconservative forces"

title: Average power
body: P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t} = \frac{W}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.2, 3.5.A.3 "average power is the total work done, divided by the time during which that work was done"

title: Instantaneous power
body: P_{\text{inst}} = \frac{dW}{dt}
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.4 "Pinst = dW/dt"

title: Instantaneous power from a constant force
body: P_{\text{inst}} = F_{\parallel} v = F v\cos\theta
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.5 "component of a constant force parallel to the object's velocity ... derived equation"

title: Power
body: Power is the rate at which energy changes with respect to time, either by transfer into or out of a system or by conversion from one type to another within a system.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.1 "Power is the rate at which energy changes with respect to time"
